summary: Evaluates five candidate protocols for the IPFIX flow export protocol against the requirements the IPFIX working group produced. It groups the candidates, scores them, and recommends choosing NetFlow v9 as the basis for IPFIX.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo compares five protocols that could carry traffic flow records out of routers, and recommends NetFlow v9 as the base for the IPFIX standard. The team sorted the candidates by design goal, by data encoding and by message flow, then checked each one against the working group's requirements.

subtitle: Five protocols for exporting network flow records are compared, and NetFlow v9 comes out on top.

tldr.problem: The IPFIX working group had to pick one protocol for exporting flow information out of routers and probes, and five different candidates had been submitted.
tldr.mechanism: An evaluation team described each candidate, grouped the five by design goal, by data encoding and by message flow, and then checked each one against the working group's requirements document.
tldr.outcome: The team recommended starting from NetFlow v9, the simplest of the five, and adding the mechanisms it lacks in transport, security, reliability and redundant configurations.

today: RFC 3955 is an Informational memo published in October 2004, and the metadata records no obsoleting or updating RFC. It documents the evaluation that recommended starting with NetFlow v9, described in RFC 3954, as the basis for the IPFIX specification.

sections.title: The Evaluation Task
sections.content:
The IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) working group was chartered to choose one protocol for exporting flow information from traffic-observing devices such as routers or dedicated probes. An evaluation team was formed to do the choosing, and every candidate came with an advocate who submitted an evaluation of that protocol against the requirements document, RFC 3917.

Five candidates were evaluated: CRANE, Diameter, LFAP, NetFlow v9 and Streaming IPDR. This document describes each of them, groups them into broad categories, checks them against specific requirements, and finally recommends one as the starting point for the work.
sections.plainLanguage: A working group needed one protocol for sending traffic records out of routers. Five were proposed, so a team compared each one against a list of requirements and picked a base to build on.

sections.title: The Five Candidate Protocols
sections.content:
CRANE carries accounting records from network elements to mediation and business support systems. The collecting server opens the connection, so the exporting side is the client, and the two exchange messages over TCP or, preferably, SCTP. The protocol defines 20 message types, negotiates templates, and carries data sequence numbers so a collector can remove duplicates after a failover.

Diameter is a generalization of RADIUS that carries authentication, authorization and accounting data as attribute/value pairs over TCP or, preferably, SCTP. Its base protocol defines fourteen command codes, organized as seven request and response pairs.

LFAP began as a flow admission protocol and later became a flow accounting protocol. It runs over TCP, knows thirteen message types, and splits each flow across two messages: a Flow Accounting Request when the flow is identified, then one or more Flow Update Notification messages later. Its data uses a Type/Length/Value format with four bytes of overhead per item.

NetFlow v9 is a generalized version of Cisco's NetFlow. The exporter sends template, option and data FlowSets to the collector over UDP, which makes it the only candidate that works over UDP. Streaming IPDR runs over TCP, either with trivial delivery or with application-layer acknowledgements, and describes its records with XML-Schema, carrying the data in XML or in the XDR encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: The five candidates come from different jobs: counting traffic fast, carrying billing records safely, or logging usage for later analysis. NetFlow v9 is the simplest of the five and the only one that can use UDP.

sections.title: Three Ways to Group the Candidates
sections.content:
The evaluation groups the protocols three ways. By design goal, NetFlow and LFAP were built for high-performance flow metering, Streaming IPDR and CRANE for carrier-grade accounting, and Diameter for general authentication, authorization and accounting.

By data representation, CRANE, IPDR and NetFlow use an external description of the data format, through templates or an XML-Schema subset, so a 32-bit integer can take just four octets. Diameter and LFAP use Type/Length/Value encodings, which let a collector decode part of the data without context but make the messages larger. CRANE is the only candidate that lets the exporter choose between big-endian and little-endian byte order.

By protocol flow, Streaming IPDR and NetFlow are mainly unidirectional, with the collector only sending acknowledgements. CRANE and LFAP are bidirectional and can negotiate templates during the session. Diameter negotiates capabilities first and then runs mostly in one direction, with Accounting-Request messages going out and Accounting-Answer messages coming back.
sections.plainLanguage: The team sorted the candidates three ways: by what they were originally built for, by how they encode data, and by which way messages travel between exporter and collector.

sections.title: Checking Each Requirement
sections.content:
Not every requirement in RFC 3917 applies to an export protocol. Several concern the metering process that feeds the exporter, so the protocol only has to report what the meter did.

On the metering side, CRANE, Diameter and IPDR treat meter reliability as out of scope and assume the meter is reliable; LFAP is the only candidate that reports data lost in the metering process. On sampling, NetFlow v9 supports it, Diameter suggests new attribute/value pairs to carry the sampling parameters, and CRANE and IPDR do not mention it at all. When the meter is overloaded, LFAP and NetFlow v9 claim to meet the requirement without expiring every existing flow, while the other three treat it as out of scope. All five support timestamps with the required one centisecond precision, but NetFlow reports them relative to the exporter's sysUpTime, and the UNIX Secs field in its header only has one second resolution.

On data transfer, all five can use IPsec and TLS at the lower layer, and all five support push mode. NetFlow v9 is the only candidate with no application-layer acknowledgements and the only one where a reliable transport is optional, so the evaluation says it needs a mapping to a congestion-friendly transport. None of the five supports anonymization, and none supports reporting the reason a flow expired.
sections.plainLanguage: The team checked the candidates one requirement at a time: sampling, overload, timestamps, reliability, security and the rest. NetFlow v9 was the simplest, and the evaluation lists what it still has to add.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
If the goal were a carrier-grade accounting protocol that could also carry IP flow information, one of CRANE, Diameter and Streaming IPDR would probably be the choice. The goal was instead to standardize existing practice in flow export, and the evaluation notes that earlier versions of NetFlow were widely implemented and used. A simple protocol that does one thing well is easy to implement, and a NetFlow collector only has to sit there and receive data.

The recommendation is to start with NetFlow v9 and add the missing mechanisms in four areas: transport, security, reliability and redundant configurations, while keeping the protocol as simple as possible. The evaluation names specific gaps. NetFlow v9 specifies no security mechanisms, so the specification must say which security protocols are used, how they are negotiated, which modes are allowed and how keys are managed. It also lacks a congestion-aware transport, so a mapping to TCP or, as suggested elsewhere, to SCTP with the Partial Reliability extension is a necessary step.

LFAP is also focused on flow export, but the evaluation says it carries too much baggage from its days as a flow admission protocol, and that its encoding is less space-efficient than that of CRANE, NetFlow or IPDR.
sections.plainLanguage: The team recommended starting from NetFlow v9 and adding the missing pieces: a congestion-friendly transport, security, reliability and support for more than one collector. The advice was to add them carefully so the protocol stays easy to implement.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security discussion of the candidates appears in Section 4.10.3 of the evaluation and is summarized here. All five candidates can use lower-layer security mechanisms such as IPsec and, apart from NetFlow v9 over UDP, TLS, and the evaluation argues that both are sufficient against the main identified threats of flow data disclosure and forgery. Diameter is the only candidate that goes into detail about how those mechanisms are applied, including negotiating certificates and ciphers in TLS and using IKE for IPsec, and it mandates that either IPsec or TLS be used.

LFAP is the only other candidate with security built in, offering four levels ranging from no security through authenticated peers to flow data authentication and encryption using HMAC-MD5-96 and DES-CBC. The evaluation says this adds little over IPsec or TLS, and notes that DES is now widely regarded as not adequately secure because its small key size makes brute-force attacks viable.
sections.plainLanguage: Every candidate could protect its traffic with IPsec or TLS, and the evaluation says that is enough against the main threats. NetFlow v9 itself says nothing about security, so the recommendation says the new specification must spell it out.

left.title: Externally described encoding
left.desc: A template or schema tells both ends the layout, so a 32-bit integer takes only four octets.

right.title: Partly self-describing encoding
right.desc: Each value carries its own type and length, so a collector can decode part of the data without context.

viz.caption: WHAT THE IPFIX SPECIFICATION STILL HAD TO ADD

items.title: Transport
items.text: Map the protocol onto a congestion-friendly transport such as TCP or SCTP.

items.title: Security
items.text: Name the security protocol, how it is negotiated, which modes are allowed and how keys are managed.

items.title: Reliability
items.text: Say how lost records are detected, how retransmission works and how failover is handled.

items.title: Redundant configurations
items.text: Support more than one collector without wasting exporter bandwidth.
